name: Isoniazid
route_note: Oral tablets or syrup, often in fixed-dose combinations with rifampicin; injectable form available.
targets: Enoyl-ACP reductase InhA (after activation by catalase-peroxidase KatG)
originator: Hoffmann-La Roche, E. R. Squibb & Sons and Bayer (independently)

discovery.by: Hoffmann-La Roche, Squibb and Bayer research groups
discovery.note: First synthesised in 1912 by Hans Meyer and Josef Mally in Prague; its anti-tuberculosis activity was discovered independently by three companies in 1951 and announced in 1952.

tagline: Inexpensive first-line TB drug that blocks mycolic acid synthesis
summary: Isoniazid is a cheap synthetic prodrug that has been a cornerstone of tuberculosis treatment and prevention since 1952. It is highly bactericidal against rapidly dividing Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and its toxicity profile is shaped by genetic differences in acetylation.
mechanism: Isoniazid is activated by the mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase KatG to an isonicotinoyl radical that combines with NAD+. The resulting adduct tightly inhibits InhA, the enoyl-acyl carrier protein reductase of the fatty acid synthase II system, blocking synthesis of mycolic acids essential for the mycobacterial cell wall.
Most clinical resistance comes from katG mutations (notably S315T), which prevent activation, or inhA promoter mutations, which cause overexpression and low-level resistance shared with ethionamide.
uses: Latent TB infection (alone, or with rifapentine or rifampicin)
TB preventive therapy in people with HIV and child contacts

history.title: First synthesis
history.detail: Hans Meyer and Josef Mally synthesise isonicotinic acid hydrazide in Prague as part of doctoral work.

history.title: Antituberculosis activity announced
history.detail: Roche, Squibb and Bayer report isoniazid's dramatic activity; press images of recovering patients at Sea View Hospital, New York follow.

history.title: Antidepressant serendipity
history.detail: The related iproniazid is observed to elevate mood, leading to the first monoamine oxidase inhibitor antidepressants.

history.title: Acetylator polymorphism
history.detail: Studies of isoniazid metabolism define slow and fast acetylator phenotypes, later linked to NAT2.

history.title: Hepatitis recognised
history.detail: An outbreak of isoniazid hepatitis among Capitol Hill workers given preventive therapy highlights hepatotoxicity.

history.title: 3HP regimen
history.detail: The PREVENT TB trial shows 12 weekly doses of isoniazid plus rifapentine are as effective as 9 months of isoniazid for latent TB.

pk.half_life: about 1 hour in fast acetylators, 2–5 hours in slow acetylators
pk.metabolism: hepatic N-acetylation by NAT2 and hydrolysis

serious: Hepatitis, occasionally fatal, increasing with age and alcohol use
Seizures and coma in overdose (treated with pyridoxine)
safety.boxed_warning: Severe and sometimes fatal hepatitis may develop, even after many months of treatment; risk is age-related and increased by daily alcohol consumption. Patients should be monitored and instructed to report symptoms (US label).

facts: Isoniazid's antituberculosis activity was discovered almost simultaneously by three companies, so none could obtain a strong product patent, keeping it cheap.
Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) is routinely co-prescribed to prevent isoniazid-induced neuropathy in at-risk people.
